Sleep and exam anxiety in first-year students: a fictional teaching paper
This paper is invented by the Appuscholar team for practice. The study, the people and the numbers do not exist.

Abstract
First-year students often report poor sleep in the weeks before examinations. We tested whether one week of a fixed bedtime routine lowered exam anxiety. Sixty first-year students from one college were randomly placed in a routine group or a waiting group. Exam anxiety was measured before and after the week. The routine group showed a larger fall in anxiety than the waiting group, t(58) = 2.36, p = .022, d = 0.61. Sleep quality and anxiety change were weakly related, r(58) = .31, p = .016. The sample was small and came from one college, so the result needs repeating.

Introduction
Exam periods are linked with short sleep and high anxiety in students (Nair & Brook, 2019). Earlier work has mostly been observational. Students who sleep badly report more anxiety, but these studies cannot say which comes first. However, very few studies have asked whether changing sleep habits for a short time changes anxiety before an exam. Little is known about what a low-cost routine, which a college could offer to every student, can achieve in one week. Rao and Dutta (2020) found that late bedtimes predicted lower marks, but they did not change bedtimes. The gap this study addresses is the lack of a controlled test of a short bedtime routine. We therefore asked whether a one-week bedtime routine lowers exam anxiety compared with no routine. We expected the routine group to show a larger drop in anxiety.

Method
Design. We used a randomised two-group design with a measurement before and after the week. Random assignment was chosen so that differences between the groups would be due to chance, and a waiting group was used because withholding the routine for one week carried little risk.

Participants. Sixty first-year students (38 women, 22 men; mean age 18.7 years, SD = 0.8) were recruited by notice board posters in one college. Students with a diagnosed sleep disorder were not included. The sample size of 60 was set by the number of students who volunteered before the deadline; no power calculation was done.

Materials. Exam anxiety was measured with a 12-item scale, the Exam Worry Scale (invented for this paper), rated from 1 to 5. Higher scores mean more anxiety. Internal consistency in this sample was good (Cronbach's alpha = .86). Sleep quality was rated with one question, scored from 1 (very poor) to 10 (very good). We chose a short scale because students were completing it during busy weeks.

Procedure. Students signed a consent form and completed the scale on paper. A coin toss decided the group for each student. The routine group were asked to go to bed within thirty minutes of a fixed time each night for seven days and to switch off screens one hour before. The waiting group were asked to keep their usual habits and were offered the routine after the study. Both groups completed the scale again on day eight. The college ethics committee approved the study. Students were told they could stop at any time.

Data processing. Paper forms were entered into a spreadsheet by one researcher and checked by a second. Two students did not return for the second measurement and were removed, leaving 58 for the analysis. Scale scores were the mean of the 12 items. Change scores were calculated as the score after minus the score before.

Statistical analysis. Change scores of the two groups were compared with an independent-samples t-test. The relationship between sleep quality and anxiety change was tested with a Pearson correlation. The significance level was .05, two-tailed. Cohen's d was reported as the effect size. We did not test for normality.

Results
Table 1. Mean anxiety change (after minus before) by group. Routine group (n = 29): M = -0.52, SD = 0.71. Waiting group (n = 29): M = -0.12, SD = 0.62. A negative change means lower anxiety. The routine group showed a larger fall in anxiety than the waiting group, t(58) = 2.36, p = .022, d = 0.61. Figure 1 shows the two group means with their ranges. Sleep quality rated after the week was weakly related to anxiety change, r(58) = .31, p = .016, so students who rated their sleep better tended to show a smaller fall in anxiety.

Discussion
The findings suggest that a short bedtime routine can lower exam anxiety within one week. This is consistent with the idea that sleep and worry affect each other. The fall of half a point on a five-point scale is modest, but it was reached with a simple routine.

Limitations
The sample was small and came from one college, so the result may not hold for other students. Anxiety was self-reported and students knew which group they were in, which may have shaped their answers. We did not measure sleep with a device. The follow-up was one week, so we do not know whether the effect lasts into the exam itself. We also did not check that the groups were similar at the start.

Recommendations
Colleges could offer a bedtime routine before examinations at little cost. Future studies should use larger and more varied samples, include a check of sleep with a device, and follow students through the examination.

Conclusion
A one-week bedtime routine was linked with a larger fall in exam anxiety than no routine in this small sample. The result needs repeating before it is used widely.

pages:
Peer tutoring and statistics anxiety: a short pasted report
This report is invented for the Appuscholar test corpus.
Abstract
We asked whether weekly peer tutoring lowers statistics anxiety in second-year psychology students. Forty-two students took part. Anxiety fell more in the tutored group than in the comparison group, and exam marks did not differ.
Method
Forty-two second-year students were recruited from two statistics classes. One class was offered weekly peer tutoring and the other was taught as usual. Anxiety was measured with a 20-item scale before and after eight weeks. The sample size was set by the class lists; no power analysis was done.
Results
The tutored group's anxiety fell more than the comparison group's, t(40) = 2.48, p = .017. Exam marks did not differ, t(40) = 0.84, p = .41. Attendance at tutoring was related to the fall in anxiety, r(19) = .52, p = .016.
References
Kumar, R., & Iyer, S. (2018). Peer learning in statistics classes. Teaching of Psychology in India, 4(2), 33-41. https://doi.org/10.5555/tpi.2018.4.2.33
Shah, M. (2021). Anxiety about numbers. Example Press.

papers.title: Night-time phone use and next-day attention
pages:
Night-time phone use and next-day attention
1. Introduction
Many students keep their phones in bed. Earlier studies linked night-time phone use with shorter sleep, but few measured attention on the next day. We asked whether phone use after midnight predicts slower reaction times the next morning.
2. Method
2.1 Participants
Thirty-six undergraduate students (20 women, 16 men; mean age 19.4 years) took part for course credit. Students who worked night shifts were not included.
2.2) Measures
Phone use was logged by an app for seven nights. Attention was measured each morning with a ten-minute reaction-time task.
1.Procedure
Students installed the app on the first evening and completed the task before their first class on each of the seven mornings.
III. Results
Phone use after midnight predicted slower reaction times, r(34) = .41, p = .013. A one-way ANOVA across three groups of phone use was significant, F(2, 33) = 4.12, p = .025.
IV Discussion
Late phone use went with slower attention the next day. The study cannot say that phone use caused the slowing.
5 References
Lee, H. (2019). Phones in bed. Sleep and Study, 3, 1-9.

papers.title: Reading aloud and word memory in Class 6
pages:
Reading aloud and word memory in Class 6
Introduction
Teachers often ask children to read new words aloud. Earlier studies with adults found a memory gain for words said aloud, called the production effect. We tested whether reading aloud can help children remember

the words a day later better than reading them silently. Twenty-four children from one school took part.
Method
Each child read twenty words aloud and twenty words silently, in a random order. The next day each child wrote down every word they could remember in five minutes.

Results
Children remembered more words read aloud (M = 9.1) than words read silently (M = 7.4), t(23) = 3.05, p = .006.
Discussion
Reading aloud helped memory in this small sample. The study used one school and one list of words, so the result needs repeating in other lessons.

papers.title: Homework time and marks
pages: Students in many schools are asked to do homework every evening, and parents often ask whether more homework leads to better marks. This invented paragraph describes a small study written without any headings, as a student might paste the text of a paper copied from a web page. Two hundred students in Class 9 from four schools kept a diary of the minutes they spent on homework for four weeks. Their mathematics and science marks at the end of the term were taken from school records with the consent of the students and their parents. Students who spent up to an hour a day on homework had higher marks than students who spent almost no time on it. Beyond an hour a day the marks did not rise any further, and students who reported more than three hours a day had slightly lower marks than those who reported one to two hours. The diaries were filled in by the students themselves, so some may have reported more time than they really spent. The schools were all in one city, and the study did not record how difficult the homework was or whether a parent or tutor helped. The authors suggest that schools set a clear limit on daily homework and that teachers check how long their tasks really take. They also point out that a diary kept for four weeks may not show what happens across a whole year, when examinations and holidays change the pattern of work. A later study could ask teachers to record the expected time for each task, compare it with the time the students report, and follow the same students for a full school year. Until then, the safest reading of these results is that a moderate amount of homework goes with better marks, and that very long hours do not seem to help. Readers should also remember that a link of this kind does not show that homework causes the higher marks; students who already do well may simply choose to spend more time on their work, and families who value schoolwork may encourage both homework and other habits that help them do well in their studies.

We asked first-year students how they study for examinations. Most reread their notes; few tested themselves. Students who tested themselves reported higher marks.

12

papers.title: Daily reading time and vocabulary growth in middle school
pages:
Daily reading time and vocabulary growth in middle school
Abstract
We followed one hundred and twenty students in Classes 6 to 8 for one
school year and asked how the minutes they read for pleasure each day
related to the growth of their vocabulary. Students kept a short daily
log, and their vocabulary was tested at the start and the end of the
year. Students who read more each day gained more words.
Introduction
Reading for pleasure is often said to build vocabulary, because books
contain many words that children rarely hear in conversation. Most of
the evidence comes from surveys that ask once how much a child reads,
and such surveys depend on memory and on what children think adults
want to hear. Daily logs are more work for students and teachers, but
they record reading close to the time it happens. Earlier log studies
were short, often a few weeks, and they rarely tested vocabulary at the
start and the end of the same period. They also asked children to note
every book by its title, which many found tiring, and so the question
remains open: does a daily log kept for a whole school year show the
same link between reading and vocabulary that the surveys report?
We expected that it would, and that the link would be stronger for the
younger students, who are still learning many common words.

Method
Students from three schools in one district took part. Each evening they
wrote down the minutes they had spent reading anything they chose, from
comics to novels, and their teachers collected the logs every Friday. A
vocabulary test of sixty words was given in the first and the last week
of the school year. The words were chosen from books written for this age
group, and the test was checked with a small pilot group of thirty other
students before the study began. Scores could range from 0 to 60, and a
second form of the test with different words was used at the end of the
year, so that students could not simply remember the first list. Nine
students moved to other schools during the year and were not included
(their logs were kept but not scored)
so the final sample was one hundred and eleven students.
Results
Minutes of daily reading were related to vocabulary gain, r(109) = .34,
p < .001. The link was stronger in Class 6 than in Class 8, but the
difference between the classes was not significant, F(2, 108) = 1.93,
p = .150.
Discussion
Students who read more each day learned more new words over the year,
and the link was clearest for the youngest students, as we expected. The
logs also showed what the students chose to read. Comics and magazines
made up almost half of the minutes in Class 6 and less than a quarter in
Class 8, where novels and books about science and sport took their place.
Teachers told us that keeping the log changed what some classes did in
the evenings, because students compared their minutes with their friends
and asked each other for books. One student wrote on the last page of his
log that he had never read so many comics in one year, and that his
mother had not believed him until she counted the pile beside his bed!
Because the logs were kept by the students, some minutes may have been
added to please the teachers, and the study cannot say that reading
caused the gain: students who already knew more words may read more.

papers.title: Handwriting and typing in lecture notes
pages:
Handwriting and typing in lecture notes
Method
Students in two lecture courses took notes either by hand on paper or by typing on a laptop for six weeks. The notes were collected after every lecture, so that we could count the words in them and compare them with the slides the lecturer had shown and with a recording of what the lecturer had said. Each student also answered ten shorter questions about the lecture at the end of each week, in the same room, at the same time and under the same rules. The questions asked for facts from the lecture and for ideas that linked two parts of it, and two markers who did not know which group a student
was in scored every answer, agreeing on nine answers out of ten before they discussed all the rest.
Students chose their own way of taking notes in the first week and kept it for the rest of the course.
Results
Handwritten notes held fewer words than typed notes in every week of the study, and they held fewer sentences copied word for word from the slides or from the lecturer. Typed notes were much longer, but most of the extra words were copied, and students who typed often wrote down whole sentences that the lecturer had said without changing a word. On the weekly questions the two groups did equally well on the short questions about facts, while the students who wrote by hand did better on the questions that asked them to link two ideas from the same lecture, a difference that was clearest in the
last two weeks, when the lectures were longest and the slides held the most new words of them all.
Students who typed said that typing was faster, and most of them would type again.

Sleep and exam anxiety in first-year students: a fictional teaching paper This paper is invented by the Appuscholar team for practice. The study, the people and the numbers do not exist.

[ page 1, Abstract ]
First-year students often report poor sleep in the weeks before examinations. We tested whether one week of a fixed bedtime routine lowered exam anxiety. Sixty first-year students from one college were randomly placed in a routine group or a waiting group. Exam anxiety was measured before and after the week. The routine group showed a larger fall in anxiety than the waiting group, t(58) = 2.36, p = .022, d = 0.61. Sleep quality and anxiety change were weakly related, r(58) = .31, p = .016. The sample was small and came from one college, so the result needs repeating.

[ page 1, Introduction ]
Exam periods are linked with short sleep and high anxiety in students (Nair & Brook, 2019). Earlier work has mostly been observational. Students who sleep badly report more anxiety, but these studies cannot say which comes first. However, very few studies have asked whether changing sleep habits for a short time changes anxiety before an exam. Little is known about what a low-cost routine, which a college could offer to every student, can achieve in one week. Rao and Dutta (2020) found that late bedtimes predicted lower marks, but they did not change bedtimes. The gap this study addresses is the lack of a controlled test of a short bedtime routine. We therefore asked whether a one-week bedtime routine lowers exam anxiety compared with no routine. We expected the routine group to show a larger drop in anxiety.

[ page 1, Method ]
Design. We used a randomised two-group design with a measurement before and after the week. Random assignment was chosen so that differences between the groups would be due to chance, and a waiting group was used because withholding the routine for one week carried little risk.

[ page 2, Method ]
Participants. Sixty first-year students (38 women, 22 men; mean age 18.7 years, SD = 0.8) were recruited by notice board posters in one college. Students with a diagnosed sleep disorder were not included. The sample size of 60 was set by the number of students who volunteered before the deadline; no power calculation was done. Materials. Exam anxiety was measured with a 12-item scale, the Exam Worry Scale (invented for this paper), rated from 1 to 5. Higher scores mean more anxiety. Internal consistency in this sample was good (Cronbach's alpha = .86). Sleep quality was rated with one question, scored from 1 (very poor) to 10 (very good). We chose a short scale because students were completing it during busy weeks.

[ page 2, Method ]
Procedure. Students signed a consent form and completed the scale on paper. A coin toss decided the group for each student. The routine group were asked to go to bed within thirty minutes of a fixed time each night for seven days and to switch off screens one hour before. The waiting group were asked to keep their usual habits and were offered the routine after the study. Both groups completed the scale again on day eight. The college ethics committee approved the study. Students were told they could stop at any time. Data processing. Paper forms were entered into a spreadsheet by one researcher and checked by a second. Two students did not return for the second measurement and were removed, leaving 58 for the analysis. Scale scores were the mean of the 12 items. Change scores were calculated as the score after minus the score before.

[ page 2, Method ]
Statistical analysis. Change scores of the two groups were compared with an independent-samples t-test. The relationship between sleep quality and anxiety change was tested with a Pearson correlation. The significance level was .05, two-tailed. Cohen's d was reported as the effect size. We did not test for normality.

[ page 3, Results ]
Table 1. Mean anxiety change (after minus before) by group. Routine group (n = 29): M = -0.52, SD = 0.71. Waiting group (n = 29): M = -0.12, SD = 0.62. A negative change means lower anxiety. The routine group showed a larger fall in anxiety than the waiting group, t(58) = 2.36, p = .022, d = 0.61. Figure 1 shows the two group means with their ranges. Sleep quality rated after the week was weakly related to anxiety change, r(58) = .31, p = .016, so students who rated their sleep better tended to show a smaller fall in anxiety.

[ page 3, Discussion ]
The findings suggest that a short bedtime routine can lower exam anxiety within one week. This is consistent with the idea that sleep and worry affect each other. The fall of half a point on a five-point scale is modest, but it was reached with a simple routine.

[ page 3, Limitations ]
The sample was small and came from one college, so the result may not hold for other students. Anxiety was self-reported and students knew which group they were in, which may have shaped their answers. We did not measure sleep with a device. The follow-up was one week, so we do not know whether the effect lasts into the exam itself. We also did not check that the groups were similar at the start.

[ page 3, Recommendations ]
Colleges could offer a bedtime routine before examinations at little cost. Future studies should use larger and more varied samples, include a check of sleep with a device, and follow students through the examination.

[ page 3, Conclusion ]
A one-week bedtime routine was linked with a larger fall in exam anxiety than no routine in this small sample. The result needs repeating before it is used widely.

Students in many schools are asked to do homework every evening, and parents often ask whether more homework leads to better marks. This invented paragraph describes a small study written without any headings, as a student might paste the text of a paper copied from a web page. Two hundred students in Class 9 from four schools kept a diary of the minutes they spent on homework for four weeks. Their mathematics and science marks at the end of the term were taken from school records with the consent of the students and their parents. Students who spent up to an hour a day on homework had higher marks than students who spent almost no time on it. Beyond an hour a day the marks did not rise any further, and students who reported more than three hours a day had slightly lower marks than those who reported one to two hours. The diaries were filled in by the students themselves, so some may have reported more time than they really spent. The schools were all in one city, and the study did not record how difficult the homework was or whether a parent or tutor helped. The authors suggest that schools set a clear limit on daily homework and that teachers check how long their tasks really take. They also point out that a diary kept for four weeks may not show what happens across a whole year, when examinations and holidays change the pattern of work. A later study could ask teachers to record the expected time for each task, compare it with the time the students report, and follow the same students for a full school year. Until then, the safest reading of these results is that a moderate amount of homework goes with better marks, and that very long hours do not seem to help. Readers should also remember that a link of this kind does not show that homework causes the higher marks; students who already do well may simply choose to spend more time on their work, and families who value schoolwork may encourage both homework and other habits that help them do well in their studies.

[ page 1, Abstract ]
We followed one hundred and twenty students in Classes 6 to 8 for one school year and asked how the minutes they read for pleasure each day related to the growth of their vocabulary. Students kept a short daily log, and their vocabulary was tested at the start and the end of the year. Students who read more each day gained more words.

[ page 1, Introduction ]
Reading for pleasure is often said to build vocabulary, because books contain many words that children rarely hear in conversation. Most of the evidence comes from surveys that ask once how much a child reads, and such surveys depend on memory and on what children think adults want to hear. Daily logs are more work for students and teachers, but they record reading close to the time it happens. Earlier log studies were short, often a few weeks, and they rarely tested vocabulary at the start and the end of the same period. They also asked children to note every book by its title, which many found tiring, and so the question remains open: does a daily log kept for a whole school year show the same link between reading and vocabulary that the surveys report?

[ page 1, Introduction ]
We expected that it would, and that the link would be stronger for the younger students, who are still learning many common words.

[ page 2, Method ]
Students from three schools in one district took part. Each evening they wrote down the minutes they had spent reading anything they chose, from comics to novels, and their teachers collected the logs every Friday. A vocabulary test of sixty words was given in the first and the last week of the school year. The words were chosen from books written for this age group, and the test was checked with a small pilot group of thirty other students before the study began. Scores could range from 0 to 60, and a second form of the test with different words was used at the end of the year, so that students could not simply remember the first list. Nine students moved to other schools during the year and were not included (their logs were kept but not scored)

[ page 2, Method ]
so the final sample was one hundred and eleven students.

[ page 2, Results ]
Minutes of daily reading were related to vocabulary gain, r(109) = .34, p < .001. The link was stronger in Class 6 than in Class 8, but the difference between the classes was not significant, F(2, 108) = 1.93, p = .150.

[ page 2, Discussion ]
Students who read more each day learned more new words over the year, and the link was clearest for the youngest students, as we expected. The logs also showed what the students chose to read. Comics and magazines made up almost half of the minutes in Class 6 and less than a quarter in Class 8, where novels and books about science and sport took their place. Teachers told us that keeping the log changed what some classes did in the evenings, because students compared their minutes with their friends and asked each other for books. One student wrote on the last page of his log that he had never read so many comics in one year, and that his mother had not believed him until she counted the pile beside his bed!

[ page 2, Discussion ]
Because the logs were kept by the students, some minutes may have been added to please the teachers, and the study cannot say that reading caused the gain: students who already knew more words may read more.
